## Adjacent field evidence -- and a variant worth noting for this ticket's scope

Observed 2026-08-05 ~01:45 UTC under parallel agent load on this store.

A completion-sidecar emit lost the race for the store write lock:

    rebar._commands._seam.CommandError: flock: could not acquire lock after 60s
    at llm/completion_sidecar.py:60 emit -> _commands/_seam.py:419 append_event

Why this is worth recording HERE specifically: this ticket describes the sidecar being
SILENTLY lost on write-lock contention, with exit 0 hiding it. In this occurrence the same
contention on the same code path surfaced LOUDLY -- a raised CommandError naming flock and
the 60s timeout, not a silent exit 0.

So there appear to be two distinct outcomes from one root condition, and any fix should
account for both: a path where the sidecar write fails loudly (this occurrence) and the
path this ticket reports where it is swallowed. Worth confirming during root-causing whether
the difference is the caller (close-gate path vs another), the lock mode, or whether the
silent case is specifically a timeout that is caught and discarded further up.

Note the affected close still completed correctly and the ticket carries both plan-review and
completion-verifier attestations -- the loss did not occur here, only the contention.

comments.body:
LIVE INSTANCE OBSERVED, 2026-08-07 — benign outcome, but the mechanism reproduced.

During a high-concurrency session (10 agents + the live Jira reconcile bridge, heavy write-lock contention with 60s flock timeouts), the ticket store was left with an ORPHANED, UNCOMMITTED COMPLETION_VERDICT sidecar:

  ?? e7a9-35fa-1d58-4095/1786105797343413001-db1d0840-315d-45a6-8319-59201a704231-COMPLETION_VERDICT.json

Measured state at the time: `git rev-list --count origin/tickets..HEAD` = 0 (nothing unpushed), working tree otherwise clean, and the ticket dir ALSO carries 1 properly tracked COMPLETION_VERDICT. So in this instance the verdict was durably recorded and the untracked file is a duplicate from a retried write — no evidence was lost.

Why it still matters for this ticket: it demonstrates the sidecar can be written OUTSIDE the commit under contention, silently and with a zero exit. Here the retry happened to also produce a committed copy. Had the retry been the one that failed, the file would have sat untracked and invisible — which is exactly this ticket's reported failure, and nothing would have reported it. The orphan is the fingerprint of the race, independent of whether that particular attempt lost data.

Corroborating symptom from the same window (recorded on 7084): a `rebar comment` failed outright with `flock: could not acquire lock after 60s`, and a push-retry logged `tickets branch push-retry merge skipped: write lock busy; push stays pending`. An agent separately reported a rejected push showing '6 unpushed commits on origin/tickets..HEAD' which had resolved by the time I measured.

Suggested acceptance-criteria strengthening: a durable-write path that leaves an untracked event file behind should be DETECTABLE — an `fsck`-style check for event files present on disk but absent from the tickets branch would turn this silent class into a reported one, and would have caught this instance regardless of the duplicate saving it.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
Measured mechanism for this ticket's silent loss, from the lock-hold instrumentation on [rebar:7084-4e33-e698-42dd] (2026-08-07). Recording here because it identifies the HOLDER that consumed the sidecar's 60s budget, which this ticket previously had to infer.

The holder is compaction, and 99% of its critical section is a read-only query. cProfile of a real `compact-on-close` on a clone of this store (71,041 commits on the tickets branch): `_compact_locked` held the store write lock for **48.1s** on a ticket with only 7 foldable events; `_build_authorship_ledger` (`compact.py:74`) accounted for 47.77s of it, and inside that `authorship.resolve_event_commit` (`attest/authorship.py:131`) accounted for 47.48s across 7 calls — **6.78s each**, one full `git log --diff-filter=A --full-history` walk of the whole tickets branch per signed event. The actual mutation (SNAPSHOT write + .retired renames + git add/commit) is ~0.4s. On a 75-event ticket the same operation held the lock for over 20 minutes.

Direct reproduction of this ticket's failure class: with one such holder running, **6 of 6 concurrent `rebar comment` writers failed at exactly 60s** (`flock: could not acquire lock after 60s`) and all six writes were permanently lost — `rebar show` afterwards contained none of them. That is the same terminal-LockTimeout path the PASS sidecar takes at `completion_sidecar.py:60`, except the sidecar swallows it at `:61-65` and returns False, which is why yours is silent and the CLI's is loud.

So the fix space for this ticket splits cleanly: shrinking the compaction critical section (proposed as R1/R2 on 7084) makes the loss far less likely, but does not change the fact that a LockTimeout destroys the write. Making the sidecar's loss non-silent (or non-lossy) is still independently needed, because at high enough concurrency any fixed budget can be exhausted. Full measurement method, hold-time table and the ranked remediation are on 7084; no fix has been implemented pending operator approval.

compiled_state.description:
# A PASS `COMPLETION_VERDICT` sidecar is silently lost on write-lock contention (exit 0, no stderr)

## Observed

Closing `d582-fd5a-7ece-4c32` (`--class flaky`) emitted a traceback ending in
`flock: could not acquire lock after 60s`, yet **exited 0** and closed and certified the ticket
correctly. The ticket is now missing its `*-COMPLETION_VERDICT.json` record. 810 tickets in this store
carry one; d582 does not.

The failing call is the PASS sidecar:

* `llm/completion_sidecar.py:60` — `append_event(...)` inside `emit()` (defined `:47`)
* called from `_commands/close_precheck.py:324` (the PASS branch; FAIL is `:310`)
* raised at `_commands/_seam.py:419`, translating `LockTimeout` from `_store/lock.py:103`
  (60s = `_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` 30 x `_DEFAULT_ATTEMPTS` 2, `lock.py:73-74`)

**It fires BEFORE the close, not after.** `close_precheck.py:324` runs inside `_completion_precheck`,
which `transition_close.py:326` calls *before* `txn.transition_core(...)` at `:343` — the documented
verify -> close -> sign order (`transition_close.py:246-252`). The STATUS and SIGNATURE writes then
succeeded seconds later (12:30:56 and 12:30:58), which is what makes the loss avoidable.

## Why it is silent — the failure is swallowed twice

`completion_sidecar.py:61-65` catches everything and returns `False`:

```python
except Exception:  # best-effort observability sidecar
    logger.warning("COMPLETION_VERDICT sidecar emit failed; continuing", exc_info=True)
    return False
```

and the caller **discards that return value** — `close_precheck.py:322-326` wraps the call in a second
try/except and never inspects it.

Best-effort is the correct POLICY: a sidecar must never fail a close. The defect is that a
**transient, retryable** failure is handled identically to a permanent one:

1. **No retry on `LockTimeout`.** One 60s attempt. Every subsequent close-path write succeeded within
   seconds. A single re-attempt, or routing the sidecar through the same lock window as
   STATUS+SIGNATURE (the `_batch_sink` seam already exists at `_seam.py:405-409`), saves the record.
2. **No machine-readable signal.** Exit stays 0, stdout is clean, and this goes only through
   `logger.warning` — unlike the drift and `SigningError` paths, which write explicit
   `Warning: closed <id> WITHOUT ...` lines to stderr (`transition_close.py:387-393`, `:404-410`).
   A `gate_error_sidecar` module exists (`llm/gate_error_sidecar.py:34` maps `"completion" ->
   "COMPLETION_VERDICT"`) and is not engaged here.

## Blast radius: metric skew, not state corruption

`COMPLETION_VERDICT` is deliberately **reducer-ignored** (`completion_sidecar.py:11-16`,
`reducer/_version.py:78`, `verify_authorship.py:378`), so compiled state, deps, validity and the
attestation are all unaffected — d582 is correctly closed and certified, and **no remediation is
needed for it**. The durable cost is observability:

* `metrics/sidecar_metrics.py:221` counts a ticket into the `first_pass_verification` denominator only
  if it has a `COMPLETION_VERDICT` record;
* `sidecar_metrics.py:106-110` counts accepted closes from `completion_verifier_pass_v1` records.

d582 silently drops out of both. The record is also **not re-emittable** — the verdict dict was
in-memory, so recovering it would need reopen -> re-close and a fresh billable verifier run.

## Not a rare race — see the amplifier

Under parallel-agent load the 60s budget is routinely exceeded, so expect silent metric drift across
many closes rather than one. The amplifier is filed separately: compact-on-close holds the store write
lock for minutes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] a `LockTimeout` on the PASS/FAIL sidecar is RETRIED at least once, or the sidecar write is routed
      into the same lock window as STATUS+SIGNATURE via the existing `_batch_sink` seam
- [ ] when the sidecar is ultimately dropped, the close writes an explicit stderr warning naming the
      ticket and what was lost, matching the existing `Warning: closed <id> WITHOUT ...` convention
- [ ] `close_precheck` stops discarding `completion_sidecar.emit`'s boolean return
- [ ] a test proves a sidecar `LockTimeout` no longer loses the record silently: it either lands after
      retry, or a stderr warning is emitted — asserted, with the lock held by the test
- [ ] the close still succeeds and stays certified when the sidecar genuinely cannot be written
      (best-effort policy preserved, verified by a test that makes the write fail permanently)

## Testing

    pytest tests/unit -k "sidecar or completion_verdict or lock" -q
    make lint && make typecheck
